subject: Biology
title: Biodiversity and Conservation
summary: The last chapter of the syllabus asks three questions: how much biological diversity exists (genetic, species and ecological diversity, the species counts for the world and for India), what patterns it follows (the latitudinal gradient and the species-area relationship), and why it is being lost and how it can be conserved (the Evil Quartet, the three arguments for conservation, in situ and ex situ methods, hotspots and sacred groves). It is a short, fact-dense chapter that the board tests through a fixed set of NCERT numbers, names and examples, so exact recall pays.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 12 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper. This chapter is the last of the three chapters of Unit X, Ecology and Environment (Organisms and Populations, Ecosystem, Biodiversity and Conservation); the unit carries about 10 marks in the current syllabus. Biodiversity and Conservation usually contributes 3 to 5 marks: one or two 1-mark items, a 2- or 3-mark question on the causes of biodiversity loss, the tropics or the two conservation approaches, and in several recent papers a 4-mark case study built on the species-area graph or on a pie chart of species numbers.

question_types.note: Who popularised the term biodiversity (Edward Wilson); which group has the most species (insects); the value of Z in the species-area relationship; what the Nile perch did in Lake Victoria; which method is ex situ (seed bank, cryopreservation, zoo) and which is in situ (sacred grove, biosphere reserve, hotspot); the number of hotspots in the world and in India; who proposed the rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich); where the sacred groves of Meghalaya are (Khasi and Jaintia Hills); which alien plant is carrot grass (Parthenium).

Why the tropics hold more species (undisturbed for millions of years, less seasonal, more solar energy); why alien species cause extinctions; why the Amazon forest is called the lungs of the planet; why cryopreservation is ex situ and not in situ; why hotspots are chosen for in situ protection (high endemism); why a fungus has more species than all vertebrates combined; why habitat fragmentation hurts large mammals and migratory birds.

Name the level of biodiversity represented by 50,000 strains of rice, 1000 varieties of mango, reserpine variation in Rauwolfia vomitoria, or estuaries and alpine meadows; define alien species invasion and name one plant and one animal invader; state why sacred groves are protected; state why the Western Ghats are a hotspot; explain the rivet popper hypothesis; give the importance of cryopreservation; distinguish in situ from ex situ conservation; state the equation of the species-area relationship and what Z means.

Three hypotheses for the greater species richness of the tropics; the species-area relationship with the graph and the equation; the importance of species diversity to ecosystem functioning with Tilman's findings; three causes of biodiversity loss (any three of the Evil Quartet) with examples; six advantages of ex situ conservation; the sixth extinction and how it differs from the earlier five; two levels of biodiversity with one example each.

The three arguments for conserving biodiversity (narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian, ethical) plus hotspots as a conservation step with the two or three Indian hotspots; the four causes of biodiversity loss in full with an NCERT example for each; in situ versus ex situ conservation in full with examples of each; the patterns of biodiversity (latitudinal gradient with the bird numbers and the three hypotheses, plus the species-area relationship with the equation).

A species-area graph (curve and log-log straight line) with questions on the equation, the meaning of C and Z and the range of Z; a passage on Lake Victoria and the Nile perch leading to questions on alien species and the Evil Quartet; the two NCERT pie charts of species numbers with questions on which sector is insects, angiosperms or fungi; a passage on a sacred grove or on the Amazon leading to questions on in situ conservation or habitat loss.

hot_topics: The Evil Quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation (Amazon, 14 to 6 per cent), over-exploitation (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon), alien species invasions (Nile perch and cichlids, Parthenium, Lantana, Eichhornia, Clarias gariepinus), co-extinctions (plant and pollinator, host and parasite)

In situ versus ex situ conservation with examples: hotspots, biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries, sacred groves versus zoos, botanical gardens, safari parks, seed banks, cryopreservation, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture
Why conserve biodiversity: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian (Amazon produces 20 per cent of oxygen, pollination, aesthetic pleasure) and ethical arguments
Species-area relationship: S = CA<sup>Z</sup>, log S = log C + Z log A, Z between 0.1 and 0.2 for small areas and 0.6 to 1.2 for whole continents, Humboldt
Latitudinal gradient and the three hypotheses for tropical richness, with the bird numbers for Colombia, New York, Greenland and India
The three levels of biodiversity with the NCERT examples (Rauwolfia vomitoria and reserpine, 50,000 strains of rice, 1000 mango varieties, Western Ghats amphibians, India versus Norway)

Numbers of species: 1.5 million described (IUCN 2004), Robert May's 7 million, animals over 70 per cent, insects over 70 per cent of animals, India 2.4 per cent of land with 8.1 per cent of species, 12 mega diversity countries

Importance of species diversity: Tilman's plots and Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis; the sixth extinction and the IUCN Red List numbers (784 species, dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller's sea cow, three tiger subspecies)

Biodiversity hotspots: 34 in the world, three in India (Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya), less than 2 per cent of land, could cut extinctions by almost 30 per cent; sacred groves of Meghalaya, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh

sections.heading: 13.1 Biodiversity: what the word means and its three levels
sections.body:
NCERT opens with an image worth keeping in mind: Class 11 taught you that the living world holds a huge range of forms, from the vast number of insect species to the four or so species of great apes. This variety at every level of biological organisation is biodiversity. The term was popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson, and it describes the combined diversity at all levels, from the genes within one species to the ecosystems of a whole region. The examiner expects exactly three levels, each with an NCERT example.

Genetic diversity is the variation a single species shows over its distributional range. Two examples are standard. The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria, growing in different Himalayan ranges, shows genetic variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine that it produces. India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1000 varieties of mango. Whenever a question mentions strains, varieties, cultivars or a chemical whose concentration differs between populations of one species, the answer is genetic diversity.

Species diversity is the diversity at the species level: the number and kinds of species in a region. NCERT's example is that the Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.

Ecological (ecosystem) diversity is the variety of ecosystems. India, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country such as Norway. When a question lists habitats or ecosystem types (estuaries, alpine meadows, mangroves), the level is ecological diversity.

Two more lines from the introduction get asked. First, the biodiversity we see today is the product of about 3.5 billion years of evolution. Second, before humans appeared, the earth's biodiversity was much larger than it is now; ever since, human activity has been destroying it. NCERT then frames the chapter around the questions that follow: how many species there are, what patterns their distribution shows, why species are being lost and how we can conserve them. Keep this frame, because the sections of the chapter follow it exactly.
sections.tip: Learn the three examples as fixed pairs: reserpine in Rauwolfia and rice strains mean genetic diversity, Western Ghats amphibians mean species diversity, India versus Norway means ecological diversity. A 2-mark question that gives two such examples and asks you to name the level is one of the commonest items from this chapter.

sections.heading: 13.1.1 How many species are there on Earth and how many in India?
sections.body:
This section is a set of numbers and the examiner wants them exactly. According to the IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million. Many more, especially in the tropics, remain undescribed, so ecologists estimate the total by a statistical comparison of the temperate-tropical species richness of a well-studied group of insects, and then extrapolate that ratio to other groups of animals and plants. Robert May made a more conservative and scientifically sound estimate of about 7 million species globally. That is the answer to the NCERT exercise 'How do ecologists estimate the total number of species present in the world?'

The proportions matter too. More than 70 per cent of all recorded species are animals; plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) make up no more than 22 per cent. Among animals, insects are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total, so out of every ten animals on the planet seven are insects. A striking comparison NCERT makes is that the number of fungal species in the world is more than the combined total of all species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals. NCERT also points out that these numbers are for the described species; the prokaryotes are not counted because conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for them and many cannot be cultured in the laboratory. If biochemical or molecular criteria were used, the diversity of prokaryotes alone might run into millions.

Now India. India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but its share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent, which makes India one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world. Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many animals have been recorded from India. Applying May's global estimate that only 22 per cent of the world's species have been recorded, India probably has more than 100,000 plant species and more than 300,000 animal species yet to be discovered and described. NCERT closes with a sobering line: it would take many more centuries to describe all these species, but a large fraction of them face the threat of becoming extinct even before they are discovered.

The two pie charts of NCERT Fig. 13.1 come from this section. Chart (a) shows the proportionate number of species of major taxa of invertebrates and vertebrates: insects are by far the largest sector; molluscs, crustaceans and other animal groups take smaller slices; and the vertebrates (fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals) together are a small sector. Chart (b) shows plants: angiosperms are the largest sector, followed by fungi, algae, lichens, mosses, ferns and allies, and gymnosperms with the smallest slice. Board papers have asked students to identify labelled sectors in these charts.
sections.tip: Write the percentages with their objects: 2.4 per cent of land, 8.1 per cent of species, 22 per cent plants, more than 70 per cent animals, more than 70 per cent of animals are insects. Students lose the mark by writing a percentage without saying what it is a percentage of.

sections.heading: 13.1.2 Patterns of biodiversity (a): latitudinal gradients
sections.body:
Biodiversity is not spread evenly across the planet; it follows patterns, and NCERT names two. The first is the latitudinal gradient: in general, species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles. With very few exceptions, the tropics (the belt between 23.5° N and 23.5° S) hold more species than temperate or polar areas. The examiner wants the bird numbers. Colombia, located near the equator, has nearly 1,400 species of birds; New York, at 41° N, has 105; and Greenland, at 71° N, has only 56. India, with much of its land in the tropical latitudes, has more than 1,200 species of birds. A forest in a tropical region like Ecuador has up to ten times as many species of vascular plants as a forest of equal area in a temperate region like the Midwest of the USA. The largest biodiversity on earth is in the tropical Amazonian rain forest of South America, home to more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles and more than 125,000 of invertebrates. Scientists estimate that this forest might hold at least two million insect species yet to be discovered.

Why do the tropics have so much more? Ecologists and evolutionary biologists have proposed several hypotheses; NCERT gives three and a 3-mark question asks for exactly these.

  1. Time for speciation. Speciation is generally a function of time. Temperate regions were subjected to frequent glaciations in the past, which repeatedly wiped out communities, whereas the tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years and so have had a long evolutionary time for species diversification.
  2. Constant, predictable environment. Tropical environments, unlike temperate ones, are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable. Such constant environments promote niche specialisation and so lead to a greater species diversity.
  3. More solar energy. There is more solar energy available in the tropics, which contributes to higher productivity; this in turn contributes indirectly to greater diversity.

When the question is 'Where would you expect more biodiversity, tropics or polar regions, and why?', name the tropics and give these three reasons. When it says 'Write any two hypotheses', give two of the three with the key words glaciation, niche specialisation and solar energy.
sections.tip: The three hypotheses are three separate reasons and the marking scheme gives one mark each. Do not merge 'less seasonal' with 'more solar energy' into one sentence; keep them as distinct points with their key words.

sections.heading: 13.1.2 Patterns of biodiversity (b): species-area relationships
sections.body:
The second pattern was found by the German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt during his pioneering explorations in the wilderness of South American jungles. Within a region, species richness increases with the area explored, but only up to a limit. The relationship between species richness and area, for a wide variety of taxa (angiosperm plants, birds, bats, freshwater fishes), turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola. On a logarithmic scale the relationship becomes a straight line, described by the equation

log S = log C + Z log A

where S is species richness, A is area, Z is the slope of the line (the regression coefficient) and C is the Y-intercept. The same relationship in ordinary form is S = CAZ. You should be able to write both forms and to name each symbol.

The examiner's favourite point is the value of Z. Ecologists have discovered that, regardless of the taxonomic group or the region, the value of Z lies in the range of 0.1 to 0.2. This is the 'significance of the slope of regression' asked in NCERT exercise 4: the slope is remarkably similar across groups and regions, which tells us that the way species richness grows with area is a general property of nature and not something special to one group. But when the species-area relationship is analysed among very large areas, such as an entire continent, the slope is much steeper, with Z values in the range of 0.6 to 1.2. For example, for frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in the tropical forests of different continents, the slope is 1.15. So the answer to 'what is the significance of the slope' has two parts: the small, consistent value for small areas within a region, and the steep value for continental comparisons.

NCERT Fig. 13.2 is the graph you must be able to draw and read. It has two curves on one set of axes: the species-area relationship on a linear scale rises steeply and then flattens (the rectangular hyperbola), and the same data plotted on log scales gives a straight line. The X-axis is Area and the Y-axis is Species richness. Board questions have presented this figure and asked for the equation of each curve, the names of the symbols and the range of Z, so learn the figure with its labels and not just the equation.

where: slope of the line, the regression coefficient; 0.1 to 0.2 for small areas, 0.6 to 1.2 for whole continents

formulas.expr: log S = log C + Z log A
where: logarithm of species richness, the straight-line form used on a log-log plot

sections.tip: The straight-line form is the one the board usually asks for, and the mark is for correctly stating that Z is the slope (regression coefficient) and C the Y-intercept. Write the range 0.1 to 0.2 and add 'regardless of the taxonomic group or the region', which is the phrase the marking scheme carries.

sections.heading: 13.1.3 The importance of species diversity to the ecosystem
sections.body:
Does the number of species in a community matter to how the ecosystem functions? For many decades ecologists believed that communities with more species were generally more stable than those with fewer species. A stable community, in NCERT's words, should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, must be either resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and must be resistant to invasions by alien species. These three features answer the old question 'List the features that make a stable biological community.'

The experimental evidence comes from David Tilman, whose long-term ecosystem experiments used outdoor plots. He found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and that in his experiments increased diversity contributed to higher productivity. Those two findings are the answer to 'Support your answer with the finding of Tilman' and to 'How did Tilman show experimentally that stability depends on species richness?' NCERT is honest that we do not yet have a definite answer to whether species richness and diversity are essential to ecosystem health, but it points out that rich biodiversity is not only essential for ecosystem health but imperative for the very survival of the human race.

The second idea is the rivet popper hypothesis of the Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich. Think of an aeroplane (the ecosystem) held together by thousands of rivets (the species). If every passenger travelling in it starts popping a rivet to take home, it may not affect flight safety at first (the ecosystem functions properly), but as more and more rivets are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak over time. Which rivet is removed also matters: a rivet on the wing (a key species that drives major ecosystem functions) is a more serious threat to flight safety than a rivet on a seat or window inside the plane. The hypothesis therefore says that the loss of a few species may not hurt at once, that cumulative losses will, and that losing a keystone species does the most damage. A 2- or 3-mark question asks you to explain the analogy and name the ecologist; make sure every part of the analogy is mapped to its ecological meaning.
sections.tip: For the rivet popper hypothesis the marks are for the mapping: aeroplane = ecosystem, rivets = species, passengers popping rivets = loss of species, rivet on the wing = key species. Writing the story without the mapping earns half.

sections.heading: 13.1.4 Loss of biodiversity: extinctions, numbers and consequences
sections.body:
The biological wealth of the planet is being lost at an alarming rate, and NCERT gives the numbers from the IUCN Red List (2004): 784 species have gone extinct in the last 500 years, made up of 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants. The named examples are the dodo (Mauritius), the quagga (Africa), the thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger, the Bali, Javan and Caspian tigers. The last twenty years alone have seen the disappearance of 27 species. Extinctions across taxa are not random: some groups such as amphibians appear to be more vulnerable. Adding to the extinct species, more than 15,500 species world-wide face the threat of extinction. Presently 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species face the threat of extinction.

The fossil record shows five episodes of mass extinction of species in the past. The sixth extinction, now in progress, is different in two ways that a 3-mark question wants: its rate is 100 to 1,000 times faster than the pre-human times, and it is caused mainly by human activities, whereas the earlier five were the result of natural causes. NCERT's warning is that if the present trends continue, nearly half of all the species on earth might be wiped out within the next 100 years.

What does the loss of biodiversity do to an ecosystem? NCERT lists three consequences, and 'How is biodiversity important for ecosystem functioning?' (exercise 6) is answered by turning them around. Loss of biodiversity in a region may lead to (i) a decline in plant production, (ii) lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought, and (iii) increased variability in certain ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles. Put with Tilman's findings and the rivet popper hypothesis, these three points make up any 3- or 5-mark answer on the importance of biodiversity to ecosystem functioning.
sections.tip: The five named extinct animals and the three tiger subspecies come with their places: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia). One-mark questions have asked for the country of one of them.

sections.heading: 13.1.4 Causes of biodiversity loss: the Evil Quartet
sections.body:
The accelerated rates of species extinction the world is facing now are largely due to human activities. NCERT names four major causes and calls them, borrowing a phrase from the evolutionary biologist Jared Diamond, the Evil Quartet. This is the single most examined part of the chapter; a 3-mark question asks for any three with an example each and a 5-mark question for all four.

(i) Habitat loss and fragmentation. This is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction. The best example is the tropical rain forests: once covering more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface, they now cover no more than 6 per cent. The Amazon rain forest, so huge that it is called the 'lungs of the planet', is being cut and cleared to cultivate soya beans or to convert to grasslands for raising beef cattle. Besides total loss, the degradation of many habitats by pollution also threatens the survival of many species. When large habitats are broken up into small fragments because of human activities, mammals and birds that require large territories and certain animals with migratory habits are badly affected, leading to population declines.

(ii) Over-exploitation. Humans have always depended on nature for food and shelter, but when 'need' turns to 'greed' it leads to over-exploitation of natural resources. Many species extinctions in the last 500 years, such as Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon, were due to over-exploitation by humans. Presently many marine fish populations around the world are over-harvested, endangering the continued existence of some commercially important species.

(iii) Alien species invasions. When alien species are introduced, unintentionally or deliberately, some turn invasive and cause the decline or extinction of indigenous species. The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in east Africa led eventually to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake. In India, the invasive weeds carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) have caused environmental damage and posed a threat to native species. The illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture purposes is posing a threat to the indigenous catfishes of Indian rivers. When asked for one plant and one animal alien species that threaten Indian natives, give Parthenium (or Lantana or Eichhornia) and Clarias gariepinus.

(iv) Co-extinctions. When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct. When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate. Another example is a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism, where the extinction of one invariably leads to the extinction of the other. This is the link the board used in 2019: mutualists tend to coevolve (the fig and its wasp from Chapter 11 is the example to quote), and the loss of one partner is a cause of biodiversity loss.
sections.tip: Name each cause with NCERT's exact label and one example. The commonest error is describing pollution as a fifth cause; NCERT places pollution under habitat degradation within habitat loss, so mention it there.

sections.heading: 13.2.1 Why should we conserve biodiversity?
sections.body:
NCERT groups the reasons for conserving biodiversity under three headings, and the 5-mark question wants all three with examples.

Narrowly utilitarian arguments are the obvious ones: humans derive countless direct economic benefits from nature. These are food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and products of medicinal importance. More than 25 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market are derived from plants, and 25,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world. Nobody knows how many more medicinally useful plants there may be in tropical rain forests waiting to be explored. With increasing resources put into bioprospecting (exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance), nations endowed with rich biodiversity can expect to reap enormous benefits. Bioprospecting is a term the examiner may ask you to define in one line.

Broadly utilitarian arguments say that biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides. The fast-dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere; NCERT asks whether we can put a price on such a service. Pollination, without which plants cannot give us fruits or seeds, is another service through bees, bumblebees, birds and bats. There are also the intangible benefits: the aesthetic pleasures of walking through thick woods, watching spring flowers in full bloom or waking up to a bulbul's song in the morning. Other ecosystem services that questions expect you to name are control of floods and soil erosion, nutrient cycling and climate regulation. When a question asks 'how is control of floods and soil erosion achieved by the biotic components' (exercise 8), the answer is that plant roots bind the soil and hold it against runoff, the canopy and litter break the force of rain, and vegetation slows and absorbs surface water so that streams do not flood.

Ethical arguments relate to what we owe to millions of plant, animal and microbe species with whom we share the planet. Philosophically or spiritually, we need to realise that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it is not of current or any economic value to us. We have a moral duty to care for their well-being and to pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.

A frequent 3-mark variant is 'Compare narrowly utilitarian and broadly utilitarian approaches'; the difference is that the first counts direct, priced products that humans take from nature, while the second counts the unpriced services that a functioning ecosystem provides to everyone.
sections.tip: Keep the three headings as three labelled paragraphs. Examiners mark this question by heading: one mark for each argument named with an example, plus marks for the numbers (25 per cent of drugs, 20 per cent of oxygen) when they appear.

sections.heading: 13.2.2 How do we conserve biodiversity? In situ conservation: hotspots, protected areas and sacred groves
sections.body:
NCERT gives two broad approaches. In situ conservation is on-site conservation: the threatened or endangered species is protected in its natural habitat, so that the entire ecosystem is protected. Ex situ conservation is off-site: the species is taken out of its natural habitat and placed in a special setting where it can be protected and given special care. The board's standard 2-mark question is the difference between the two, and the standard 5-mark question wants each described with examples.

When we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all three levels is protected. Faced with the conflict between development and conservation, many nations find it unrealistic and economically not feasible to conserve all their biological wealth, so the number of species waiting to be saved has to be prioritised. Conservationists have identified biodiversity hotspots: regions with very high levels of species richness and a high degree of endemism (species confined to that region and found nowhere else). Initially 25 hotspots were identified; nine more were added later, bringing the total to 34. Three of these hotspots, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya, cover our country's exceptionally high biodiversity regions. These hotspots are also regions of accelerated habitat loss. Although all the hotspots put together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area, the number of species they collectively harbour is extremely high, and strict protection of them could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent. That is why the Western Ghats are a hotspot: very high species richness, high endemism (for example, of amphibians) and rapid habitat loss.

In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries. NCERT's figures are 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries. India has also a long history of religious and cultural traditions that emphasised protection of nature: in many cultures tracts of forest were set aside and all the trees and wildlife within them were venerated and given total protection. These are sacred groves, found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh. In Meghalaya the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants. Their role in conservation is that religious sentiment gives total protection to every organism inside, so they preserve species that have vanished elsewhere. Sacred groves are in situ conservation, and a question that pairs a sacred grove with a botanical garden is asking you to contrast in situ with ex situ.
sections.tip: Learn the three Indian hotspots with their exact NCERT names, including 'and Sri Lanka' after Western Ghats. For sacred groves, name the state with the region: Khasi and Jaintia Hills, Meghalaya is the one asked most.

sections.heading: 13.2.2 Ex situ conservation and the international efforts
sections.body:
In ex situ conservation the threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in a special setting where they can be protected and given special care. Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose. Many animals that have become extinct in the wild continue to be maintained in zoological parks. Ex situ conservation has moved well beyond keeping threatened species in enclosures. Now the gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods by cryopreservation techniques (storage at very low temperature, in liquid nitrogen at about −196 °C), eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods. Seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants are kept for long periods in seed banks. Pollen banks store pollen in the same way, and gene banks hold the genetic material of many strains.

The 2019 board paper asked for six advantages of the ex situ approach, and the list to give is: (1) threatened animals and plants get protection and special care outside the dangers of their habitat; (2) animals extinct in the wild survive in zoos and can later be reintroduced; (3) gametes of threatened species can be stored by cryopreservation for long periods; (4) eggs can be fertilised in vitro, which allows captive breeding; (5) plants can be multiplied rapidly by tissue culture; (6) seed banks preserve many genetic strains of commercially important plants. Each advantage is one marking point, so write them as a numbered list.

The difference from in situ conservation is that in situ protects the species together with its whole ecosystem and is cheaper and more natural, while ex situ protects the individual species intensively and can rescue species whose habitat is already gone. Exam answers should say that in situ is the better approach where the habitat survives and ex situ is the fallback when it does not.

Biodiversity knows no political boundaries, and its conservation is a collective responsibility of all nations. Two international efforts are in NCERT. The historic Convention on Biological Diversity ('The Earth Summit') held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for the conservation of biodiversity and the sustainable utilisation of its benefits. In a follow-up, the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa, saw 190 countries pledge their commitment to achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss at global, regional and local levels. A 1-mark item may ask the place and year of either summit, so learn both pairs.
sections.tip: Cryopreservation, seed banks, tissue culture and in vitro fertilisation are all ex situ. If a question says the species is protected 'in its natural habitat', it is in situ; if it says 'in a special setting', it is ex situ. Assertion-Reason items test exactly this.

key_terms.definition: The combined diversity of life at all levels of biological organisation, from the genes within a species to the ecosystems of a region; the term was popularised by Edward Wilson.

The genetic variation a single species shows over its distributional range, for example the differing potency and concentration of reserpine in Rauwolfia vomitoria populations of the Himalaya, or the 50,000 strains of rice in India.
The diversity at the species level, the number and kinds of species in a region; the Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.
The diversity at the ecosystem level; India, with deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has greater ecosystem diversity than Norway.
One of the 12 countries that together hold the largest share of the world's species; India is one, with 2.4 per cent of the land area and 8.1 per cent of the global species diversity.
The pattern that species diversity decreases as one moves away from the equator towards the poles, so that the tropics hold far more species than temperate or polar regions.
Humboldt's observation that within a region species richness increases with area up to a limit, following a rectangular hyperbola, S = CA<sup>Z</sup>, or log S = log C + Z log A on a log scale.

The slope of the straight line in the log species-area relationship; it lies between 0.1 and 0.2 for small areas regardless of taxonomic group or region, and between 0.6 and 1.2 for very large areas such as continents.

Paul Ehrlich's analogy in which an ecosystem is an aeroplane, species are its rivets, and losing rivets weakens the plane, with a rivet on the wing (a key species) mattering far more than one on a seat.
The mass extinction now in progress, occurring at a rate 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times and caused mainly by human activities, unlike the five earlier natural episodes.
The four major causes of biodiversity loss: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions.
The breaking of a large habitat into small pieces by human activity, which badly affects mammals and birds that need large territories and animals with migratory habits.

The introduction of a non-native species, deliberately or unintentionally, that turns invasive and causes the decline or extinction of indigenous species, as the Nile perch did to the cichlids of Lake Victoria.
The extinction of a species whose survival depends obligately on another that has become extinct, such as a host fish's unique parasites or one partner of a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism.
The condition of a species being confined to a particular region and found nowhere else; a high degree of endemism is one of the two criteria for a biodiversity hotspot.

A region with very high species richness, a high degree of endemism and accelerated habitat loss; 34 exist in the world, of which Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya cover parts of India.

On-site conservation, in which a threatened species is protected within its natural habitat so that the whole ecosystem is protected, as in hotspots, biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries and sacred groves.

Off-site conservation, in which threatened plants and animals are taken out of their natural habitat and protected in a special setting such as a zoological park, botanical garden, safari park, seed bank or cryopreservation facility.

A tract of forest set aside by religious or cultural tradition in which all trees and wildlife are venerated and given total protection, found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.
Preservation of gametes, embryos or other living material in viable and fertile condition for long periods by storing them at very low temperature in liquid nitrogen; an ex situ technique.
The exploration of molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance, such as new drugs.

The benefits a functioning ecosystem provides without a price, such as oxygen production, pollination, control of floods and soil erosion, nutrient cycling and aesthetic pleasure; the basis of the broadly utilitarian argument.
The Convention on Biological Diversity held at Rio de Janeiro in 1992, which called on all nations to conserve biodiversity and use its benefits sustainably.
The 2002 summit at Johannesburg, South Africa, where 190 countries pledged to achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the rate of biodiversity loss at global, regional and local levels.

formula_sheet.name: Species-area relationship
formula_sheet.expr: S = CA<sup>Z</sup>; on a log scale log S = log C + Z log A
formula_sheet.note: S species richness, A area, C the Y-intercept, Z the slope (regression coefficient). Z = 0.1 to 0.2 for small areas regardless of taxon or region; 0.6 to 1.2 for whole continents; 1.15 for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents. Found by Alexander von Humboldt.

formula_sheet.name: Global species numbers
formula_sheet.expr: IUCN (2004): a little over 1.5 million species described; Robert May's estimate about 7 million
formula_sheet.note: More than 70 per cent of recorded species are animals; plants (algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms) 22 per cent. Insects are over 70 per cent of animals. Fungal species outnumber all fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals combined.

formula_sheet.name: India's share
formula_sheet.expr: 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, 8.1 per cent of global species diversity
formula_sheet.note: One of 12 mega diversity countries. About 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species recorded. By May's 22 per cent rule, over 100,000 plant and 300,000 animal species remain to be described.

formula_sheet.name: Latitudinal gradient in birds
formula_sheet.expr: Colombia (near equator) about 1,400 species; India more than 1,200; New York (41° N) 105; Greenland (71° N) 56
formula_sheet.note: Species diversity falls from the equator to the poles. Amazon rain forest: over 40,000 plants, 3,000 fishes, 1,300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, 378 reptiles, over 125,000 invertebrates.

formula_sheet.name: Three hypotheses for tropical richness
formula_sheet.expr: Time (tropics undisturbed for millions of years, temperate regions glaciated) · Constancy (less seasonal, predictable, promotes niche specialisation) · Energy (more solar energy, higher productivity)
formula_sheet.note: Give all three for a 3-mark question, each with its key word.

formula_sheet.name: Tilman's findings
formula_sheet.expr: More species → less year-to-year variation in total biomass; increased diversity → higher productivity
formula_sheet.note: Long-term outdoor plot experiments. The evidence for species richness giving stability to a community.

formula_sheet.name: Extinction numbers (IUCN Red List 2004)
formula_sheet.expr: 784 species extinct in the last 500 years: 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants; 27 species lost in the last 20 years; more than 15,500 species under threat
formula_sheet.note: Under threat now: 12 per cent of birds, 23 per cent of mammals, 32 per cent of amphibians, 31 per cent of gymnosperms. Sixth extinction is 100 to 1,000 times faster than pre-human rates.

formula_sheet.name: Named extinct species
formula_sheet.expr: Dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia), Bali, Javan and Caspian tiger subspecies
formula_sheet.note: Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon are the examples of over-exploitation; the others illustrate recent extinctions.

formula_sheet.name: The Evil Quartet with examples
formula_sheet.expr: Habitat loss and fragmentation (Amazon; rain forests from 14 to 6 per cent of land) · Over-exploitation (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon, marine fish) · Alien species (Nile perch and 200 cichlids of Lake Victoria; Parthenium, Lantana, Eichhornia; Clarias gariepinus) · Co-extinctions (host and parasite, plant and pollinator)
formula_sheet.note: The phrase Evil Quartet comes from Jared Diamond; habitat loss is the most important cause.

formula_sheet.name: Three arguments for conservation
formula_sheet.expr: Narrowly utilitarian (food, fibre, drugs: over 25 per cent of drugs from plants, 25,000 plant species in traditional medicine, bioprospecting) · Broadly utilitarian (ecosystem services: Amazon gives 20 per cent of oxygen, pollination, aesthetic value) · Ethical (intrinsic value of every species, moral duty to future generations)
formula_sheet.note: Five-mark answer; write three labelled paragraphs.

formula_sheet.name: Hotspots
formula_sheet.expr: 34 in the world (25 initially, 9 added); three in India: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya
formula_sheet.note: Criteria: very high species richness plus high endemism; also regions of accelerated habitat loss. Together under 2 per cent of land; strict protection could cut mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.

formula_sheet.name: India's protected areas and sacred groves
formula_sheet.expr: 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 wildlife sanctuaries (NCERT figures)
formula_sheet.note: Sacred groves: Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghats (Karnataka, Maharashtra), Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar (Madhya Pradesh). All in situ.

formula_sheet.name: Ex situ methods
formula_sheet.expr: Zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation of gametes, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture propagation, seed banks
formula_sheet.note: Six advantages were asked in CBSE 2019; list one per line.

formula_sheet.name: International summits
formula_sheet.expr: Earth Summit (Convention on Biological Diversity), Rio de Janeiro, 1992 · World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg, 2002, 190 countries, target 2010
formula_sheet.note: One-mark items ask the place and the year.
